To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
overwintered queen hornets frequently visit decayed logs of trees, and release parasitic nematodes there in late June to mid-Auguest.
the parasitic Sphaerularia nematode manipulatively causes overwintered queens to visit decayed log hibernation sites to release juvenile nematodes.
the parasitic worm manipulates its hornet host to visit decay logs in the summer for transmission.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the transmission of S. vespae from the host hornet to the next generation of the nematode.
the behavior of the host and the parasite in a parasitic system.
the behavior of hornet queens in summer and the nematode’s manipulation of its host to transmit itself.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the parasitic behavior of Sphaerularia vesparum in its host is a result of manipulation by the nematode.
the nematode S. vespae is transmitted from one generation of hornets to the next by the manipulation of its host, V. simillima.

the parasitic S. vespae manipulates its host, V. simillima, to visit decayed log sites for nematode release, which occurs at the same time as the emergence of the juvenile nematodes from the hosts’ bodies, and thus facilitates the transmission of the nematode.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the nematode S. vespae is transmitted to hornet queens by a unique route, which has not been found for any other nematode species.

the nematode S. vespae manipulates the host hornet to release its juveniles at a site where the nematode can survive, and the host queen, deprived of its fertility, is compelled to visit the same site in summer for the nematode’s transmission.

the parasitic behavior of nematodes is not limited to the manipulation of host behavior for the nematodes’ transmission, but that it also includes the manipulation of host habitat selection for the nematode’s transmission.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the parasitic behavior of the nematode S. vespae may be the first example of a parasitic manipulation of the behavior of a social host.
the parasitic manipulation of the host is not always to the host’s detriment.
the nematode has evolved a novel strategy for its transmission, which is to induce the host to visit a suitable habitat for nematode release.
